newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli leader calls for fast-paced talks.
newsitem.headline: Israeli leader calls for fast-paced talks.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu urged Palestinians on Wednesday to break a peacemaking deadlock and race into talks on the tough issues yet to be negotiated.

Faced with a stalemate in talks after he sent bulldozers to start a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem, Netanyahu told CNN International he would begin building an adjacent housing project for Arabs within two weeks.

"I have offered -- and I think this is important to consider -- that we should engage in final-settlement negotiations -- in fact not delay them, but expedite them," the Israeli leader said in Jerusalem.
"I know that there are people who believe that this could never happen. They believe that we'll never achieve a solution. I beg to differ," he said.

The tough "final-settlement" issues include the Palestinian refugees, Jewish settlers in occupied lands, borders and the future of East Jerusalem, captured by Israel in 1967 and annexed but claimed by both sides.
The right-wing leader, elected 11 months ago, said having more issues on the table all at once would afford negotiators greater flexibility in peacemaking.

He has previously proposed concluding talks on these issues in six to nine months, an initiative which Palestinians rejected as aiming to avoid implementing Israeli interim pullbacks in the West Bank under peace deals already signed.
Appearing on the same programme, Jordan's King Hussein, whose country made peace with Israel in 1994, said the building of Jewish settlements on occupied Arab land only helped to foster distrust.
But Netanyahu said he had an answer for critics of his construction of the Har Homa Jewish settlement in East Jerusalem which he began in March on a hilltop Palestinians call Jabal Abu Ghneim.
"Within the next two weeks we will begin construction for Arab housing alongside the construction we have already done. We are absolutely committed for that equal treatment," he said.

-- His government had on Wednesday begun a process of letting 56,000 Palestinian workers enter Israel, lifting a closure imposed following a guerrilla attack in March. He insisted Israel wanted to ease Palestinians' economic burdens.

-- Israel would work to ensure unimpeded access to Jerusalem's holy places for Christians, Moslems and Jews. He said he favoured a policy "of religious sovereignty if you will, incorporated in our negotiations for a final settlement."

-- His government was looking into making it easier for East Jerusalem Arabs to regain the residency rights which Israeli authorities have been revoking after they leave the city. Human rights groups have accused the Jewish state of quietly trying to deport thousands of Palestinian residents of East Jerusalem in a bid to tighten its grip on all of the city.

Both Middle East leaders embraced the notion of conducting Arab-Israeli negotiations out of the public eye, the monarch even addressing Netanyahu by his nickname at one point when he said: "Bibi, I think maybe we can do something, all of us, to see if we can move away from the public scene."
Netanyahu responded: "Your Majesty, my friend, I think you're right. It would be wonderful if we could find the opportunity to really discuss things discreetly."
